title: Terminology
body_md:
Below we use several descriptive but not
generally accepted names. The quantity \eqref{sum:law}, that is, the supremum over $x$ of the sum of $|h_k(x)|^q$
over indices $k\le N$, is called the \emph{power kernel}, and the estimate \eqref{eq:blockkernel} of the
same sum over a dyadic block of indices $M\le k<2M$ is called the \emph{block estimate}. By a
\emph{critical point} we mean the value $p=4/3$ (or $s=4/3$) at which a logarithmic factor
appears in the estimate. The standard lower bound for the error will be called the
\emph{two-point estimate}: if the functions $g$ and $-g$ of the class, with admissible errors,
correspond to the same data, then the error of any recovery operator is at least
$\|g\|_\infty$ (Section~\ref{diagonal}).

label: sum:point
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: pointwise estimates

title: Proof
body_md:
The Hermite polynomials of \cite{Muckenhoupt1970} are defined by a
generating function and coincide with \eqref{herm} by \cite[(5.5.3), (5.5.7)]{Szego}, and the
function $\mathcal H_k$ of \cite[(2.1)]{Muckenhoupt1970} is our $h_k$. By
\cite[(2.3)]{Muckenhoupt1970}, where this estimate is derived from the table
\cite[p.~700]{AskeyWainger1965}, there exist absolute constants $C,\gamma>0$ such that
for all $k\ge0$
$$
|h_k(x)|\le C\bigl(\lambda_k^{1/3}+|x^2-\lambda_k|\bigr)^{-1/4}\ \ (x^2\le2\lambda_k),
\qquad
|h_k(x)|\le Ce^{-\gamma x^2}\ \ (x^2>2\lambda_k).
$$
In the second case $\lambda_k^{1/3}+x^2-\lambda_k\le2x^2$ and $e^{-\gamma x^2}\le C_\gamma(2x^2)^{-1/4}$;
this gives \eqref{sum:env}. Estimate \eqref{sum:envmax} follows from \eqref{sum:env}, since
$\lambda_k^{1/3}\ge(k+1)^{1/3}$. By \cite[(8.91.10), p.~242]{Szego}
$\max_{x\in\mathbb R}e^{-x^2/2}|H_k(x)|\cong(2^{k}k!)^{1/2}c_0k^{-1/12}$ with a constant $c_0>0$;
division by $(2^{k}k!\sqrt\pi)^{1/2}$ gives \eqref{sum:maxlow} for $k\ge k_0$, and the finitely many
remaining indices are absorbed into the constant, since $h_k\not\equiv0$. $\Box$

label: lem:blockest
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: block estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
For $s=1$, by \eqref{sum:envmax} we have
$|h_k(x)|\le CM^{-1/12}=CM^{\bar a(1)}$, since $a(1)=-\frac14<b(1)=-\frac1{12}$. Let
$s>1$, that is, $q<\infty$. On the block $\lambda_k^{1/3}\ge M^{1/3}$, and the same count as in the
proof of Theorem \ref{sum:kernel}, together with a comparison with an integral, gives
$$
\sum_{M\le k<2M}|h_k(x)|^q\le2C^q\sum_{j=0}^{M}\bigl(M^{1/3}+j\bigr)^{-q/4}
\le C\left\{
\begin{array}{ll}
M^{1-q/4},& q<4,\\[1mm]
\log(2+M),& q=4,\\[1mm]
M^{(4-q)/12},& q>4 .
\end{array}
\right.
$$
Since $qa(s)=1-q/4$ and $qb(s)=(4-q)/12$, taking the $q$-th root gives
\eqref{eq:blockkernel}: $M^{a(s)}$ for $s>4/3$, $(\log(2+M))^{1/4}$ for $s=4/3$ and
$M^{b(s)}$ for $s<4/3$. $\Box$
head: manual

label: lem:tail
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:tail}
Let $1\le s\le\infty$, $\mu>\max\{0,\bar a(s)\}$ and $f\in W_s^\mu$. Then the series
\eqref{function} converges absolutely and uniformly on $\mathbb R$, its sum is continuous, and for
every $N\ge1$
$$
\|f-S_N f\|_\infty\le c\|f\|_{s,\mu}N^{-(\mu-\bar a(s))}L_s(N) ,
$$
where $c$ depends only on $s$ and $\mu$.
head: environment

label: eq:tailsum
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $K\ge0$, $M=K+1$ and $E_i=\{k:2^{i}M\le k<2^{i+1}M\}$, $i\ge0$;
these blocks partition $\{k>K\}$. On $E_i$ we have $\underline k=k\ge2^{i}M$, so the
$\ell_s$ norm of the coefficients $(a_k(f))_{k\in E_i}$ does not exceed $(2^{i}M)^{-\mu}\|f\|_{s,\mu}$.
H\"older's inequality at a fixed $x$ (for $s=1$ and $s=\infty$, the product of a sum and a
maximum) and \eqref{eq:blockkernel} give
$$
\sum_{k\in E_i}|a_k(f)h_k(x)|\le C\|f\|_{s,\mu}(2^{i}M)^{-(\mu-\bar a(s))}L_s(2^{i}M) .
$$
For $s\ne4/3$ the sum over $i$ is a geometric progression with ratio
$2^{-(\mu-\bar a(s))}<1$. For $s=4/3$ we have $\bar a(s)=0$ and $2+2^{i}M\le(2+M)^{i+1}$, so that
$L_s(2^{i}M)\le(i+1)^{1/4}L_s(M)$, and the series $\sum_i(i+1)^{1/4}2^{-i\mu}$ converges. In both cases
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tailsum}
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\sum_{k>K}|a_k(f)h_k(x)|\le C\|f\|_{s,\mu}(K+1)^{-(\mu-\bar a(s))}L_s(K+1).
\end{equation}
The right-hand side tends to zero as $K\to\infty$, so the series \eqref{function} converges
absolutely and uniformly, and its sum is continuous as a uniform limit of continuous partial
sums. For $K=N$ estimate \eqref{eq:tailsum} gives the statement of the lemma, since
$(N+1)^{-(\mu-\bar a(s))}\le N^{-(\mu-\bar a(s))}$ and $L_s(N+1)\le2L_s(N)$. $\Box$
head: manual

label: lem:smooth
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:smooth}
Let $1\le s\le\infty$, $\mu>0$ and $f\in W_s^\mu$. Then for every method of
$\mathcal S^\theta$ with $\theta>\mu-\bar a(s)$ and for every $N\ge1$
$$
\|S_N f-S_N^\nu f\|_\infty
\le cC(\nu)\|f\|_{s,\mu}N^{-(\mu-\bar a(s))}L_s(N) ,
$$
where $c$ depends only on $s$, $\mu$ and $\theta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $k=0$ condition \eqref{qual} gives $\nu_0^N=1$, and the term with
$k=0$ in the difference $S_N f-S_N^\nu f=\sum_{k=0}^N(1-\nu_k^N)a_k(f)h_k$ vanishes. Let
$I=\lfloor\log_2N\rfloor$ and $B_i=\{k\le N:2^i\le k<2^{i+1}\}$, $i=0,\ldots,I$. On $B_i$ we have
$\underline k=k\ge2^i$ and $|1-\nu_k^N|\le C(\nu)2^\theta2^{i\theta}N^{-\theta}$. As in the
proof of Lemma \ref{lem:tail}, H\"older's inequality and \eqref{eq:blockkernel} with $M=2^i$
give
$$
\sum_{k\in B_i}|(1-\nu_k^N)a_k(f)h_k(x)|
\le CC(\nu)\|f\|_{s,\mu}N^{-\theta}2^{it}L_s(2^i),
\qquad t=\theta-\mu+\bar a(s)>0 .
$$
Since $L_s(2^i)\le L_s(N)$ and $\sum_{i\le I}2^{it}\le(1-2^{-t})^{-1}2^{It}\le CN^t$,
we obtain $\|S_N f-S_N^\nu f\|_\infty\le cC(\nu)\|f\|_{s,\mu}N^{t-\theta}L_s(N)$, as
required. $\Box$
head: manual

label: lem:noise
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $0\le k\le N$ condition \eqref{qual} gives
$|1-\nu_k^N|\le C(\nu)(k/N)^\theta\le C(\nu)$, whence $|\nu_k^N|\le1+C(\nu)$. The right-hand side of
\eqref{ModVer} is linear in the input sequence, so
$S_N^\nu f-S_N^\nu\mathbf f^\delta=-\sum_{k=0}^N \nu_k^N \xi_k h_k$, and at a fixed
$x$ H\"older's inequality gives
$$
\Bigl|\sum_{k=0}^N \nu_k^N \xi_k h_k(x)\Bigr|
\le\bigl(1+C(\nu)\bigr)\|\mbox{\boldmath$\xi$\unboldmath}\|_{\ell_p}\Bigl(\sum_{k=0}^N|h_k(x)|^{p'}\Bigr)^{1/p'} ;
$$
the supremum over $x$ gives the first inequality in \eqref{eq:sigma}. The second inequality follows from Theorem
\ref{sum:kernel} with $q=p'$: for $p<4/3$ we have $p'>4$ and $K_{N,p'}\asymp1$, for $p=4/3$,
$K_{N,4}\asymp\log(2+N)$, for $p>4/3$, $K_{N,p'}^{1/p'}\asymp(N+1)^{3/4-1/p}
\le2^{a(p)}N^{a(p)}$; for $p=1$ estimate \eqref{sum:envmax} suffices. $\Box$
head: manual

label: thm:accuracy
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:accuracy}
Let $1\le s\le\infty$, $1\le p\le\infty$, $\mu>\max\{0,\bar a(s)\}$, let
\eqref{perturbation} hold, and let a method of $\mathcal S^\theta$ have $\theta>\mu-\bar a(s)$.
Then for every $f\in W_s^\mu$ and every $N\ge1$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:acc}
\|f-S_N^\nu\mathbf f^\delta\|_\infty
\le c\bigl(N^{-(\mu-\bar a(s))}L_s(N)+\delta N^{a_+(p)}L_p(N)\bigr) ,
\end{equation}
and if $\gamma_1 \delta^{-1/\rho}\le N\le\gamma_2 \delta^{-1/\rho}$ for some
$0<\gamma_1 \le\gamma_2$, then
$$
\|f-S_N^\nu\mathbf f^\delta\|_\infty\le c\,\delta^{e_{\mathrm{tr}}}
\qquad(s\ne4/3,\ p\ne4/3),
$$
$$
\|f-S_N^\nu\mathbf f^\delta\|_\infty
\le c\,\delta^{e_{\mathrm{tr}}}\bigl(\log(\mathrm e/\delta)\bigr)^{1/4}
\qquad(s=4/3\ \text{or}\ p=4/3) .
$$
The constants depend only on $s$, $p$, $\mu$, $\theta$, $C(\nu)$, $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$. In
particular, the level $N_*=\lceil\delta^{-1/\rho}\rceil$ satisfies this condition with
$\gamma_1=1$, $\gamma_2=2$, and the method uses $N_*+1\le3\delta^{-1/\rho}$ perturbed
Fourier--Hermite coefficients.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemmas \ref{lem:tail}, \ref{lem:smooth} and \ref{lem:noise},
\eqref{eq:fullError} gives \eqref{eq:acc} for every $N\ge1$ and every
$0<\delta<1$.

Now let $\gamma_1 \delta^{-1/\rho}\le\allowbreak N\le\allowbreak\gamma_2 \delta^{-1/\rho}$. The left
inequality gives $N^{-(\mu-\bar a(s))}\le\gamma_1^{-(\mu-\bar a(s))}\delta^{e_{\mathrm{tr}}}$, and the right one gives
$\delta N^{a_+(p)}\le\gamma_2^{a_+(p)}\delta^{1-a_+(p)/\rho}
=\gamma_2^{a_+(p)}\delta^{e_{\mathrm{tr}}}$, since
$$
1-\frac{a_+(p)}{\rho}=\frac{\rho-a_+(p)}{\rho}
=\frac{\mu-\bar a(s)}{\rho}=e_{\mathrm{tr}} .
$$
This equality means that with this choice of $N$ both terms in \eqref{eq:acc} have the
same order $\delta^{e_{\mathrm{tr}}}$. For $s\ne4/3$ and $p\ne4/3$ all logarithmic factors
equal one. Let $s=4/3$ or $p=4/3$. Since $\delta^{-1/\rho}>1$, we have
$2+N\le(2+\gamma_2)\delta^{-1/\rho}$, whence
$\log(2+N)\le C'\log(\mathrm e/\delta)$ with $C'=\max\{1,\log(2+\gamma_2),1/\rho\}$. Therefore
$L_s(N),L_p(N)\le(C')^{1/4}(\log(\mathrm e/\delta))^{1/4}$, and each term in
\eqref{eq:acc} carries at most the power $1/4$ of the logarithm.

Finally, $t=\delta^{-1/\rho}>1$, so $t\le N_*\le t+1\le2t$ and $N_*+1\le2t+1\le3t$;
method \eqref{ModVer} uses the data only for $k=0,1,\ldots,N_*$. $\Box$
head: manual

label: rem:technique
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:technique}\rm
The upper bounds of Lemmas \ref{lem:tail}, \ref{lem:smooth}, \ref{lem:noise} and of Theorem
\ref{thm:accuracy} are obtained not by the standard scheme used, for example, in
\cite[Theorem~3.1]{MathePereverzev2002} (for $s=p=2$ for systems with
$\|\varphi_k\|_\infty\asymp k^{\beta}$, $\beta\ge0$) and in \cite{Sol_Stas_UMZ2022},
\cite{SemSol_Sim}, \cite{SolodkyVolynets2026}.
In the standard scheme each term is first bounded
by the maximum of its Hermite function, $|h_k(x)|\le\|h_k\|_\infty$, and only then summed over $k$ by
means of H\"older's inequality. Here H\"older's inequality is applied at a fixed $x$
to the whole block of indices, and the supremum over $x$ is taken after the summation: the quantities
\eqref{sum:law}, \eqref{eq:blockkernel} and \eqref{eq:sigma} are computed for
the block as a whole. Already for unit weights this changes the order for $1\le q\le12$ (for $q>12$
both sums below are bounded): by Lemma \ref{sum:point} and Theorem \ref{sum:kernel}, for
$1\le q<\infty$
$$
\sum_{k=0}^N\|h_k\|_\infty^q\asymp\sum_{j=1}^{N+1}j^{-q/12},
\qquad
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\sum_{k=0}^N|h_k(x)|^q\asymp\sum_{j=1}^{N+1}j^{-q/4},
$$
since the maximum of the function $h_k$ is attained near the point
$x_k\approx\sqrt{2k+1}$: outside the strip $|x^2-2k-1|\le A(2k+1)^{1/3}$ the bound \eqref{sum:env}
is smaller than \eqref{sum:maxlow} for a sufficiently large absolute constant $A$.

The standard scheme leads to the following estimates. Set
$$
\tilde\beta=\mu-\Bigl(\frac{11}{12}-\frac1s\Bigr),
\qquad
\tilde a(p)=\max\Bigl\{\frac{11}{12}-\frac1p,\,0\Bigr\},
\qquad
\tilde e=\frac{\tilde\beta}{\tilde\beta+\tilde a(p)} .
$$
For $\mu>\max\{0,11/12-1/s\}$ and a method of $\mathcal S^\theta$ with $\theta>\tilde\beta$ it gives, for
every $N\ge1$,
$$
\|f-S_N^\nu\mathbf f^\delta\|_\infty
\le c\bigl(N^{-\tilde\beta}+\delta N^{\tilde a(p)}\tilde L_p(N)\bigr),
$$
where $\tilde L_p(N)=(\log(2+N))^{1/12}$ for $p=12/11$ and $\tilde L_p(N)=1$ for $p\ne12/11$, and,
for $N\asymp\delta^{-1/(\tilde\beta+\tilde a(p))}$, the estimate $c\,\delta^{\tilde e}$ for
$p\ne12/11$ and $c\,\delta(\log(\mathrm e/\delta))^{1/12}$ for $p=12/11$. Here
$\tilde e=(\mu+1/s-11/12)/(\mu+1/s-1/p)$ for $p>12/11$ and $\tilde e=1$ for $p<12/11$.

Let us compare these estimates with Theorem \ref{thm:accuracy}. By \eqref{exps} we have
$$
\frac{11}{12}-\frac1s-\bar a(s)=
\left\{
\begin{array}{ll}
\frac16, & s>4/3,\\[1mm]
\frac23\bigl(1-\frac1s\bigr), & s<4/3,
\end{array}
\right.
\qquad
\tilde a(p)-a_+(p)=
\left\{
\begin{array}{ll}
\frac16, & p>4/3,\\[1mm]
\frac{11}{12}-\frac1p, & 12/11<p<4/3,\\[1mm]
0, & p\le12/11 ,
\end{array}
\right.
$$
hence $\tilde\beta\le\beta$ and $\tilde a(p)\ge a_+(p)$. Moreover, the condition
$\mu>\max\{0,11/12-1/s\}$ implies $\mu>\max\{0,\bar a(s)\}$, and every method with $\theta>\beta$
also satisfies the condition $\theta>\tilde\beta$, so that for $\mu>\max\{0,11/12-1/s\}$ and
$\theta>\beta$ both estimates
refer to the same method. The comparison below is made for $s\ne4/3$ and $p\ne4/3$, where
the estimate of Theorem \ref{thm:accuracy} contains no factors $L_s$ and $L_p$. Since $t/(t+a)$ increases in $t>0$ and decreases in
$a\ge0$, we have $\tilde e\le e_{\mathrm{tr}}$, the inequality being strict for $p>12/11$, while for
$p=12/11$ the standard scheme loses a logarithmic factor. For $p<12/11$ both estimates
have order $\delta$, but the standard scheme needs $\asymp\delta^{-1/\tilde\beta}$
coefficients, while the method of Theorem \ref{thm:accuracy} with the level $N_*$ needs $\asymp\delta^{-1/\beta}$; these orders
coincide only for $s=1$.

By Theorem \ref{thm:diag}\,(i), (iii) the order $\delta^{e_{\mathrm{tr}}}$ is not improved by any finite
diagonal method, and the methods $\mathcal S^\theta$ with $\theta>\beta$ attain it. Therefore
the difference of the exponents is a loss caused by the standard estimation scheme, and not a property of the method.
For comparison, in
\cite{SolodkyVolynets2026} the same scheme gave the exact order (ibid., Lemma~2.1 and
Theorem~4.7), since for the Laguerre functions the sum of a block of $N$ functions with indices from
$[N,3N]$ has order $N$ in the weighted uniform norm, that is, the order of the sum of its
maxima: the lower bound is given in Lemma~4.1 of the same paper, and the upper bound $CN$ follows
from the uniform boundedness of the Laguerre functions (ibid., (2.4)). For the Hermite functions the sum of maxima over such a block
$\Omega$ has order $N^{11/12}$, whereas by Theorem \ref{sum:kernel} with $q=1$ and
Lemma \ref{lem:block}\,{\rm(i)}
$$
\max_{\varepsilon_k=\pm1}\Bigl\|\sum_{k\in\Omega}\varepsilon_k h_k\Bigr\|_\infty\asymp N^{3/4} .
$$
head: environment

label: lem:block
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Items (i) and (ii) are derived from two asymptotic formulas of Szeg\"{o}: in
the oscillatory region for (i) and near the turning point for (ii). At the chosen point the main
term of the formula is bounded away from zero in absolute value, and the remainder term is small for $N\ge N_0$; item (iii)
follows by direct substitution.

Set $\lambda_k=2k+1$. Formula (8.22.8) of \cite{Szego}, after
division by $(2^k k!\sqrt\pi)^{1/2}$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{pr}
h_k(x)=A_k \Bigl\{\cos\Bigl(\lambda_k^{1/2}x-\frac{k\pi}2\Bigr)
+\frac{x^3}6\,\lambda_k^{-1/2}\sin\Bigl(\lambda_k^{1/2}x-\frac{k\pi}2\Bigr)+R_k(x)\Bigr\},
\end{equation}
where $A_k=\Gamma(k+1)\Gamma(k/2+1)^{-1}(2^k k!\sqrt\pi)^{-1/2}$ and $|R_k(x)|\le Bk^{-1}$ uniformly on the interval $[0,1]$ with an absolute constant $B$.
The duplication formula $\Gamma(k+1)=\pi^{-1/2}2^k \Gamma((k+1)/2)\Gamma(k/2+1)$ gives
$A_k^2=\pi^{-1}\Gamma((k+1)/2)/\Gamma(k/2+1)$, and the log-convexity of the gamma function gives
$\Gamma(k/2+1)^2\le\Gamma((k+1)/2)\,\Gamma(k/2+3/2)=\frac{k+1}2\,\Gamma((k+1)/2)^2$. Therefore
for every $k\ge1$ we have $A_k\ge\pi^{-1/2}((k+1)/2)^{-1/4}\ge\pi^{-1/2}k^{-1/4}$.

We prove (i). Let $k\in[N,3N]$ be an integer. The point $x_0\le19/50$ belongs to $[0,1]$, and the quantity
$\varphi_k=\lambda_k^{1/2}x_0=\kappa_0((2k+1)/N)^{1/2}$, by $2<(2k+1)/N\le7$, satisfies
$\pi/6<\kappa_0\sqrt2=0.537\ldots<\varphi_k\le\kappa_0\sqrt7=1.005\ldots<\pi/3$.
For $k=2m$ we have $\cos(\varphi_k-k\pi/2)=(-1)^m\cos\varphi_k$, and for $k=2m+1$ it equals
$(-1)^m\sin\varphi_k$. On $[\pi/6,\pi/3]$ both functions $\cos t$ and $\sin t$ are at least $1/2$;
therefore the main term in the braces of \eqref{pr} is at least $1/2$ in absolute value. Since $x_0\le19/50$ and
$\lambda_k\ge1$, the second term does not exceed $\frac16(19/50)^3<10^{-2}$, and for $N\ge5B$ we have
$|R_k(x_0)|\le B/N\le1/5$. Consequently, $|h_k(x_0)|\ge A_k(\frac12-10^{-2}-\frac15)>A_k/4$,
and the estimate of $A_k$ gives \eqref{bulkpoint}. For $\varepsilon_k=\operatorname{sign}h_k(x_0)$ all
terms $\varepsilon_k h_k(x_0)=|h_k(x_0)|$ are nonnegative, and the norm bounds the value at a
point from above. Since $\Omega$ consists of $N$ indices not exceeding $3N$, we obtain \eqref{bulksum}.

We prove (ii). Theorem~8.22.9 of \cite{Szego} in the normalization \eqref{herm} gives
\begin{equation}\label{airyexp}
h_k(x)=\gamma_{\mathcal A}\,k^{-1/12}\bigl\{\mathcal A(t)+O(k^{-2/3})\bigr\},
\qquad
x=\lambda_k^{1/2}-2^{-1/2}3^{-1/3}k^{-1/6}t .
\end{equation}
Here $t=2^{1/2}3^{1/3}k^{1/6}(\lambda_k^{1/2}-x)$ is the parameter that gives the position of $x$
relative to the point $\lambda_k^{1/2}$. The formula is uniform in $|t|\le1$, where
$\gamma_{\mathcal A}>0$ is an absolute constant; the constant in the remainder
is denoted by $B'$. The function $\mathcal A(t)$ is the Airy function of Section~1.81 of the same book. It
is continuous, and by its power series $\mathcal A(0)=\pi/(3\Gamma(2/3))>0$. By continuity
there is $\eta>0$ such that $|\mathcal A(t)-\mathcal A(0)|<\mathcal A(0)/2$ for $|t|<\eta$.
Taking $t_0=\min\{1,\eta/2\}$, we obtain $\mathcal A(t)\ge\mathcal A(0)/2$ for $0\le t\le t_0$;
the number $t_0$ is absolute, since the function $\mathcal A$ is fixed.

Set $\tau=t_0/\sqrt3$ and $J=\lfloor\tau N^{1/3}\rfloor$. For $N\ge\tau^{-3}$ we have
$u=\tau N^{1/3}\ge1$, so $J\ge1$ and $J\ge u/2$ (for $1\le u<2$ this is obvious,
and for $u\ge2$ it follows from $\lfloor u\rfloor>u-1\ge u/2$). Moreover,
$\tau\le1/\sqrt3$ and $N\ge6$, whence $J\le\tau N^{1/3}\le N/2\le N-1$. We split the $2N+1$ integers of the interval $[N,3N]$ into
consecutive intervals of at most $J$ numbers each; there are at most
$(2N+1)/J+1\le3N/J$ of them, so one of them contains at least $J/3\ge\kappa N^{1/3}$ points of
$\Omega$, where $\kappa=\tau/6$. Denote the set of these points by $W$, and let
$k_*=\min W$; then $0\le k-k_*<J\le\tau N^{1/3}$ for $k\in W$.

Set $x_W=\lambda_{k_*}^{1/2}$. Substituting $x=x_W$ into the expression for $t$ after
\eqref{airyexp}, we obtain $t_k=2^{1/2}3^{1/3}k^{1/6}(\lambda_k^{1/2}-\lambda_{k_*}^{1/2})$.
Since $k\ge k_*$ and $\lambda_k=2k+1$, we have $t_k\ge0$. From
$\lambda_k^{1/2}+\lambda_{k_*}^{1/2}>2(2N)^{1/2}$ and $k\le3N$ it follows that
$$
t_k=2^{1/2}3^{1/3}k^{1/6}\,\frac{2(k-k_*)}{\lambda_k^{1/2}+\lambda_{k_*}^{1/2}}
<2^{1/2}3^{1/3}(3N)^{1/6}\,\frac{\tau N^{1/3}}{(2N)^{1/2}}
=\sqrt3\,\tau=t_0 .
$$
Thus $0\le t_k<t_0\le1$, and to $t=t_k$ the estimate
$\mathcal A(t)\ge\mathcal A(0)/2$ chosen above applies. The remainder in \eqref{airyexp} does not exceed
$B'k^{-2/3}\le\mathcal A(0)/4$ for $k\ge(4B'/\mathcal A(0))^{3/2}$. Hence for $k\in W$,
taking into account $k\le3N$,
$$
|h_k(x_W)|\ge\tfrac14\gamma_{\mathcal A}\mathcal A(0)\,k^{-1/12}\ge c_1N^{-1/12},
\qquad c_1=\tfrac14\,3^{-1/12}\gamma_{\mathcal A}\mathcal A(0) .
$$

We prove (iii). By the orthonormality of the system $\{h_k\}$ the coefficients of the function $f$ from (iii)
are equal to $(3N)^{-\mu}N^{-1/s}\varepsilon_k$ on $\Omega$ and to zero outside $\Omega$.
On $\Omega$ we have $\underline k=k\le3N$, and for $\mu>0$ this gives
$\underline k^{\,\mu}|a_k(f)|\le N^{-1/s}$; therefore $\|f\|_{s,\mu}\le(N\cdot N^{-1})^{1/s}=1$
for $s<\infty$ and $\|f\|_{\infty,\mu}\le1$. The norm bounds the value at the point $x_0$ from above, and by
\eqref{bulksum}
$$
\|f\|_\infty\ge(3N)^{-\mu}N^{-1/s}\sum_{k\in\Omega}|h_k(x_0)|
\ge\frac{3^{-1/4}}{4\sqrt\pi}\,3^{-\mu}N^{-\mu+3/4-1/s},
$$
which gives \eqref{blocktail}, since $3^{-1/4}(4\sqrt\pi)^{-1}=0.107\ldots$

We add that all restrictions on $N$ are satisfied for $N\ge N_0$, where
$$
N_0=\lceil\max\{5B,\ \tau^{-3},\ (4B'/\mathcal A(0))^{3/2}\}\rceil .
$$
This is an absolute number, since
the constants $B$ and $B'$ of the remainder terms in \eqref{pr} and \eqref{airyexp} and the number $t_0$
are absolute.
$\Box$

label: rem:wellposed
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:wellposed}\rm
Following \cite[\S\,2.8]{LuP}, we call a problem well-posed if its solution can be approximated with
accuracy of order $O(\delta)$. Let $\mu>\max\{0,\bar a(s)\}$, as in Theorem~\ref{thm:diag}.
Theorem~\ref{thm:diag}\,(ii), (iii) implies that for $1\le p<4/3$ and $s\ne4/3$ the problem of
summation of the Fourier--Hermite series from perturbed coefficients in the metric of ${\cal L}_\infty(\mathbb R)$ is well-posed: here $e_{\mathrm{tr}}=1$,
so that
$$
c\,\delta\le\mathcal E_\delta(W_s^\mu,\Psi,C(\mathbb R),\ell_p)\le C\,\delta ,
$$
and the order $\delta$ is attained by every method of the class $\mathcal S^\theta$ with $\theta>\beta$ at the
truncation level $N_*$. The reason is that for $p<4/3$ the data error is not amplified:
the last part of estimate \eqref{eq:sigma} of Lemma~\ref{lem:noise} does not depend on $N$. For $p>4/3$
we have $e_{\mathrm{tr}}<1$, and the order $\delta$ is attained by no finite diagonal
method (Theorem~\ref{thm:diag}\,(i)), and for $s\ge4/3$ by no recovery
operator either (Theorem~\ref{thm:diag}\,(ii)), so that the problem is ill-posed. For $s<4/3<p$
this conclusion is established only for finite diagonal methods. For $p=4/3$
or $s=4/3$ a logarithmic factor remains between the bounds of Theorem~\ref{thm:diag}. For
comparison: in the problem of summation of Fourier--Laguerre series in the weighted uniform metric
\cite{SolodkyVolynets2026} well-posedness holds only for $p=1$.
